telencephalon (cerebrum).teach: Paired cerebral hemispheres: cortex, subcortical white matter (association, commissural and projection fibres), the basal ganglia and the lateral ventricles. Lobes are separated by the central and sylvian fissures; eloquent territory includes the precentral (motor), postcentral (sensory) and dominant peri-sylvian language cortex, with the internal capsule carrying the corticospinal tract deep to the insula.
telencephalon (cerebrum).surg: Access is tailored to lobe and depth. Convexity and gyral lesions: navigation-guided craniotomy with cortical and subcortical mapping, done awake for dominant peri-sylvian, insular or motor lesions. Deep and paraventricular targets: trans-sulcal tubular or trans-cortical corridors, or an anterior interhemispheric trans-callosal route to the body of the lateral ventricle. Insular lesions: trans-sylvian or trans-cortical with lenticulostriate awareness. Pitfalls: the motor strip and corticospinal tract, the arcuate/superior longitudinal fasciculus for language, the optic radiations in temporal/occipital work, and bridging veins on interhemispheric approaches.
telencephalon (cerebrum).ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

diencephalon.teach: Thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus and subthalamus framing the third ventricle. The thalamus relays sensorimotor and limbic loops and abuts the posterior limb of the internal capsule laterally; the hypothalamus governs endocrine and autonomic function.
diencephalon.surg: Deep and highly eloquent. Anterior third-ventricular and thalamic targets: interhemispheric trans-callosal trans-foraminal or trans-choroidal corridors. Posterior/pineal-region and posterior thalamic targets: supracerebellar-infratentorial or occipital trans-tentorial routes. Pitfalls: the fornix and internal cerebral veins around the foramen of Monro, the internal capsule laterally, and hypothalamic injury with endocrine and autonomic sequelae.

midbrain.teach: Mesencephalon: tectum (superior and inferior colliculi), tegmentum and paired cerebral peduncles, with the nuclei of CN III (interpeduncular) and CN IV (dorsal, decussating). Traversed by the cerebral aqueduct.
midbrain.surg: Intrinsic lesions are entered through defined safe zones: the anterior mesencephalic (perioculomotor) zone via pterional/orbitozygomatic or trans-sylvian; the lateral mesencephalic sulcus via subtemporal; and the supracollicular/intercollicular zones via supracerebellar-infratentorial. Pitfalls: oculomotor and trochlear function, and the deep venous complex of the pineal region.

pons.teach: Ventral pons (corticospinal and corticopontine fibres, pontine nuclei) and dorsal tegmentum housing the nuclei of CN V-VIII. On the rhomboid fossa the facial colliculus overlies the abducens nucleus and the genu of the facial nerve.
pons.surg: Safe-entry zones guide the approach: the peritrigeminal and lateral zones via retrosigmoid for ventrolateral lesions; the suprafacial and infrafacial triangles via a midline telovelar/trans-fourth-ventricular route for dorsal lesions. Pitfalls: the facial colliculus (must be avoided), CN VI and VII, and the corticospinal tracts, with continuous cranial-nerve and MEP monitoring.

medulla oblongata.teach: Contains cardiorespiratory centres, the nuclei of CN IX-XII, the pyramidal decussation ventrally and the dorsal-column nuclei; forms the lower floor of the fourth ventricle.
medulla oblongata.surg: Very low tolerance for injury. Dorsal/exophytic lesions: midline suboccipital-telovelar exposure using the posterior median sulcus or a postpyramidal/posterolateral sulcus entry. Anterolateral lesions: far-lateral approach. Mandatory IONM. Pitfalls: the obex and area postrema, the lower cranial nerves, and the vertebral artery/PICA.
medulla oblongata.ref: Youmans & Winn (8th ed); Kobayashi, Neurosurgery of Complex Vascular Lesions and Tumors.

cerebellum.teach: Vermis and hemispheres, with cortex, deep nuclei (dentate and others) and three peduncles connecting to the brainstem; together with the tela and velum it roofs the fourth ventricle.
cerebellum.surg: Midline suboccipital for vermian and fourth-ventricular lesions using the telovelar route (opening the cerebellomedullary fissure) to spare the vermis; paramedian/lateral suboccipital for hemispheric lesions; supracerebellar-infratentorial for the tentorial and pineal surface. Pitfalls: PICA and its branches, the deep nuclei, and posterior-fossa CSF and pressure dynamics.

spinal cord.teach: Conveys the corticospinal (motor), dorsal-column (proprioception/vibration) and spinothalamic (pain/temperature) tracts; paired roots exit at each segment, and the cervical cord supplies the upper limbs. Blood supply is from the anterior spinal artery and paired posterior spinal arteries.
spinal cord.surg: Intramedullary lesions: midline myelotomy through the posterior median sulcus (splitting the dorsal columns) or a dorsal-root-entry-zone myelotomy for eccentric lesions, after laminotomy/laminoplasty exposure. Continuous D-wave, MEP and SSEP monitoring. Pitfalls: dorsal-column and corticospinal injury and preservation of the anterior spinal artery.

atlas (c1 vertebra).teach: Ring-shaped first cervical vertebra with no body; paired lateral masses articulate above with the occipital condyles (nodding) and below with the axis (rotation). The vertebral artery grooves the superior surface of the posterior arch.
atlas (c1 vertebra).surg: Exposed in far-lateral and posterior craniovertebral approaches; C1 lateral-mass screws anchor occipitocervical and atlantoaxial constructs. Pitfalls: the V3 vertebral-artery segment in the sulcus arteriosus of the posterior arch, and the C2 nerve root with its surrounding venous plexus.

axis (c2 vertebra).teach: Second cervical vertebra bearing the odontoid process (dens), the pivot for atlantoaxial rotation, stabilised by the transverse and alar ligaments.
axis (c2 vertebra).surg: Central to atlantoaxial fixation: C2 pedicle, pars (Magerl transarticular) or translaminar screws, and anterior odontoid screw fixation for selected dens fractures. Pitfalls: a high-riding/medialised vertebral artery that precludes pars or pedicle screws, and canal encroachment.

_vertebra.teach: Typical subaxial cervical vertebra: body anteriorly, paired pedicles and laminae forming the arch, transverse foramina transmitting the vertebral artery (C6 up to C1), and uncovertebral joints laterally.
_vertebra.surg: Anterior cervical (Smith-Robinson) approach for discectomy/corpectomy and fusion; posterior lateral-mass (Roy-Camille/Magerl) or subaxial pedicle screws for fixation; laminectomy or laminoplasty for decompression. Pitfalls: the vertebral artery in the transverse foramen, the exiting nerve roots, and the recurrent laryngeal nerve on anterior approaches.

occipital bone.teach: Forms the foramen magnum and much of the posterior and inferior skull base: the squamous part (posterior-fossa wall), the condylar part (occipital condyles) and the basiocciput (clivus), which meets the sphenoid.
occipital bone.surg: Landmark for suboccipital craniotomy/craniectomy and foramen-magnum decompression (e.g. Chiari); the condyle is partially drilled in the far-lateral/transcondylar approach to widen the ventral corridor to the lower clivus and craniovertebral junction. Pitfalls: the transverse and sigmoid sinuses and torcula on the squamous part, and the hypoglossal canal and condylar emissary vein at the condyle.

right vertebral artery.teach: Ascends the transverse foramina from C6 to C1, loops over the posterior arch of the atlas, then pierces the dura to join its fellow as the basilar artery.
right vertebral artery.surg: The V3 loop is the key hazard in far-lateral, transcondylar and C1-2 instrumentation. Identify before condylar drilling or C1 lateral-mass screws.
right vertebral artery.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

left vertebral artery.teach: Often the dominant vertebral artery; same V1-V4 course to the vertebrobasilar junction.
left vertebral artery.surg: Dominance influences the side chosen for a far-lateral approach and the safety of any sacrifice.
left vertebral artery.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

skull.teach: The cranial vault and skull base: frontal, parietal, temporal, sphenoid and occipital bones meeting at sutures, with the pterion (fronto-parieto-temporo-sphenoidal junction) as the thinnest point of the lateral vault.
skull.surg: Determines every craniotomy. Landmarks: pterion for the frontotemporal flap; asterion overlying the transverse-sigmoid junction for retrosigmoid; inion and superior nuchal line for suboccipital. Pitfalls: dural venous sinuses beneath asterion/inion, and the middle meningeal artery grooving the inner table at pterion.
skull.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

mandible.teach: The lower jaw, articulating at the temporomandibular joint; its ramus and condyle lie immediately anterior to the external auditory canal.
mandible.surg: Relevant to transmandibular and transcervical exposures of the clivus and upper cervical spine; mandibular subluxation widens the corridor in high anterior approaches.
mandible.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

right common carotid.teach: Ascends in the carotid sheath with the internal jugular vein and vagus nerve, bifurcating near the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (about C3-4).
right common carotid.surg: Defines the anterior cervical approach: the plane is developed medial to the carotid sheath. Pitfalls: carotid injury, and retraction damage to the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerves.
right common carotid.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

left common carotid.teach: Arises directly from the aortic arch (unlike the right, from the brachiocephalic trunk), then follows the same cervical course in the carotid sheath.
left common carotid.surg: Same anterior cervical considerations as the right; the left approach carries a longer, more vulnerable recurrent laryngeal nerve course in the tracheo-oesophageal groove.
left common carotid.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

right internal carotid.teach: Continues from the bifurcation without cervical branches, entering the carotid canal and passing through the cavernous sinus to supply the anterior circulation.
right internal carotid.surg: Central to skull-base and cavernous-sinus work; the petrous and paraclinoid segments are exposed in transpetrosal and anterior clinoidectomy approaches. Injury is potentially fatal.
right internal carotid.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

left internal carotid.teach: Mirror-image vessel supplying the left anterior circulation via its cavernous and supraclinoid segments.
left internal carotid.surg: Same skull-base considerations as the right; proximal control in the neck is planned before cavernous or paraclinoid exposure.
left internal carotid.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

right internal jugular vein.teach: Drains the sigmoid sinus through the jugular foramen and descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid artery.
right internal jugular vein.surg: Usually the dominant drainage side; occlusion risks venous infarction. At risk in jugular-foramen and far-lateral approaches, alongside cranial nerves IX-XI.
right internal jugular vein.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

left internal jugular vein.teach: Contralateral venous drainage from the sigmoid sinus via the jugular foramen.
left internal jugular vein.surg: Assess dominance before sacrificing either side; the non-dominant vein is more tolerant of ligation.
left internal jugular vein.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

_craniotomy.teach: Schematic bone flap footprint projected onto the outer table of the skull, drawn from surface landmarks.
_craniotomy.surg: APPROXIMATE TEACHING SCHEMATIC ONLY - not a template for planning or navigation. Actual flap position is set intraoperatively from the patient's own landmarks, imaging and navigation.
_craniotomy.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

brain surface (skull-stripped).teach: Skull-stripped, de-faced brain surface of a single de novo glioblastoma case (UPenn-GBM sub-002), shown for spatial context. Facial and skull anatomy were removed at source.
brain surface (skull-stripped).surg: Orientation reference only. Measured against the atlas centre, this lesion lies in the RIGHT hemisphere, roughly at the mid-coronal level and about 18 mm below centre — a right temporal / posterior peri-insular location.
brain surface (skull-stripped).ref: UPenn-GBM cohort, Bakas et al., Scientific Data 2022 (CC BY 4.0); TCIA.

enhancing tumour.teach: Contrast-enhancing rim on post-gadolinium T1, marking blood-brain-barrier breakdown at the proliferating tumour margin (about 28 mL here).
enhancing tumour.surg: The enhancing margin is the conventional target for maximal safe resection, and the completeness of its removal is the resection measure most consistently linked with outcome. For this right temporal lesion the exposure is a temporal (or frontotemporal) craniotomy; 5-ALA fluorescence highlights this compartment. Protect Meyer's loop and the optic radiation in the temporal stem, and the vessels of the sylvian fissure.
enhancing tumour.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

necrotic / non-enhancing core.teach: Central non-enhancing necrotic cavity within the enhancing rim - a defining feature of glioblastoma on imaging. Approximately 15 mL here.
necrotic / non-enhancing core.surg: Debulked early to create working space and reduce mass effect; internal decompression of the core makes the enhancing margin easier to mobilise away from eloquent tissue.
necrotic / non-enhancing core.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

peritumoural oedema / flair hyperintensi.teach: T2/FLAIR hyperintense territory around the tumour, roughly 169 mL in this case. It represents vasogenic oedema together with infiltrating tumour cells, which extend well beyond the enhancing margin.
peritumoural oedema / flair hyperintensi.surg: Because this zone contains infiltrating tumour, supramarginal (supratotal) resection beyond the enhancing rim is debated as a way to improve survival - constrained by proximity to eloquent cortex and white-matter tracts. Its bulk also drives mass effect and is the target of perioperative dexamethasone.
peritumoural oedema / flair hyperintensi.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

region_frontal.teach: Frontal-lobe glioblastoma. The frontal lobe tolerates resection comparatively well, but the posterior margin abuts the precentral gyrus and the supplementary motor area medially.
region_frontal.surg: Frontal or frontotemporal (pterional) craniotomy. Map the precentral gyrus before resecting posteriorly. SMA resection can cause a transient akinesia-and-mutism syndrome that usually recovers. On the LEFT, add language mapping for posterior inferior frontal (Broca) involvement. Watch the anterior cerebral and callosomarginal vessels medially.
region_frontal.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

region_fronto-temporal / peri-sylvian.teach: Lesion straddling the frontal and temporal opercula around the sylvian fissure.
region_fronto-temporal / peri-sylvian.surg: Frontotemporal (pterional) craniotomy with wide sylvian dissection. On the LEFT this is dominant-hemisphere territory: awake mapping for language is the default. Preserve the middle cerebral branches crossing the fissure and the arcuate/superior longitudinal fasciculus deep to the opercula.
region_fronto-temporal / peri-sylvian.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

region_insular / peri-sylvian.teach: Insular glioblastoma, deep to the frontal, temporal and parietal opercula and lateral to the lentiform nucleus.
region_insular / peri-sylvian.surg: Among the most demanding locations. Trans-sylvian or transcortical-transopercular routes after wide fissure opening. The lenticulostriate arteries define the medial limit of safe resection; the internal capsule lies immediately medial. Awake mapping on the dominant side; MCA branches (M2/M3) must be preserved as they cross the insular surface.
region_insular / peri-sylvian.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

region_temporal.teach: Temporal-lobe glioblastoma, related to the temporal horn, hippocampus and the optic radiation running in the temporal stem.
region_temporal.surg: Temporal craniotomy. Non-dominant lesions tolerate wider anterior temporal resection; on the DOMINANT side limit posterior extension and map language. Meyer's loop is the principal visual risk — injury produces a contralateral superior quadrantanopia. Identify the temporal horn early as a landmark, and protect the basal vein and vein of Labbé.
region_temporal.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

region_parietal.teach: Parietal glioblastoma, adjacent to the postcentral gyrus, the superior longitudinal fasciculus and the optic radiation.
region_parietal.surg: Parietal craniotomy with sensory and motor mapping anteriorly. Dominant-side inferior parietal resection risks acalculia, agraphia and other Gerstmann features; non-dominant risks hemispatial neglect. The optic radiation runs deep — visual field loss is common with deep resection.
region_parietal.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

region_occipital.teach: Occipital glioblastoma involving or abutting the primary visual cortex around the calcarine sulcus.
region_occipital.surg: Occipital craniotomy, often with an interhemispheric or supratentorial-infraoccipital trajectory. Visual field loss is the expected trade-off and should be discussed explicitly beforehand. Protect the superior sagittal and transverse sinuses at the margins, and the calcarine and posterior cerebral branches.
region_occipital.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

region_occipito-temporal.teach: Lesion at the occipito-temporal junction, involving fusiform and lingual territory and the posterior optic radiation.
region_occipito-temporal.surg: Occipito-temporal or subtemporal exposure. High risk to the optic radiation and, on the dominant side, to reading and naming networks (fusiform). Vein of Labbé injury during temporal retraction is a classic and avoidable cause of venous infarction.
region_occipito-temporal.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

region_deep / thalamic-basal ganglia.teach: Deep-seated glioblastoma of the thalamus or basal ganglia, immediately adjacent to the internal capsule and ventricular system.
region_deep / thalamic-basal ganglia.surg: Often biopsy rather than resection. Where resection is attempted, corridors include transcallosal-transventricular, transsulcal (with a tubular retractor) or transcortical routes chosen by the lesion's own axis. The internal capsule and lenticulostriate/thalamoperforating vessels are the limiting structures; hydrocephalus may need CSF diversion.
region_deep / thalamic-basal ganglia.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

region_posterior fossa / midline.teach: Posterior-fossa or midline lesion related to the cerebellum, fourth ventricle and brainstem.
region_posterior fossa / midline.surg: Midline or paramedian suboccipital craniotomy; the telovelar route reaches the fourth ventricle while sparing the vermis. Manage CSF and posterior-fossa pressure carefully, protect PICA, and watch for postoperative lower-cranial-nerve and swallowing problems.
region_posterior fossa / midline.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); Figueiredo (ed.), Brain Anatomy and Neurosurgical Approaches.

reference brain surface.teach: Shared reference brain. Every lesion in these libraries is registered to the same atlas space, so positions and volumes are directly comparable on one brain.
reference brain surface.surg: Use it to compare corridors and tumour phenotypes side by side. Each lesion is labelled with its location or molecular class and carries the matching approach considerations.

mol_gbm idh-wt g4.teach: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4 — the classic phenotype: a thick irregular enhancing rim around central necrosis, with extensive surrounding T2/FLAIR signal. In this case roughly 19 mL enhancing, 8 mL necrotic and 198 mL T2/FLAIR abnormality.
mol_gbm idh-wt g4.surg: Maximal safe resection of the enhancing component, then chemoradiotherapy. MGMT promoter methylation predicts temozolomide benefit and is the key molecular result to have before adjuvant decisions. 5-ALA aids identification of the enhancing compartment. Median survival remains of the order of 15 months despite complete resection.
mol_gbm idh-wt g4.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); WHO Classification of CNS Tumours, 5th ed (2021).

mol_astro idh-mut g4.teach: Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 4 — grade 4 by necrosis, microvascular proliferation or CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion, yet biologically distinct from IDH-wildtype glioblastoma. Here necrosis dominates (about 172 mL) with almost no enhancement.
mol_astro idh-mut g4.surg: Same operative principle of maximal safe resection, but prognosis is substantially better than IDH-wildtype disease, which justifies a more aggressive pursuit of complete resection in accessible territory. Under WHO 2021 this is no longer called glioblastoma — the distinction changes both counselling and trial eligibility.
mol_astro idh-mut g4.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); WHO Classification of CNS Tumours, 5th ed (2021).

mol_astro idh-mut g3.teach: Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 3. Note the absence of any enhancing component — the tumour is defined entirely by T2/FLAIR abnormality (about 105 mL here), which is typical and a reason enhancement alone is a poor guide to grade in IDH-mutant disease.
mol_astro idh-mut g3.surg: Because there is no enhancing target, resection is planned against the T2/FLAIR volume, and the extent of that resection correlates with survival. Intraoperative ultrasound or iMRI helps, since the margin is invisible under white light. Adjuvant radiotherapy plus PCV or temozolomide follows.
mol_astro idh-mut g3.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); WHO Classification of CNS Tumours, 5th ed (2021).

mol_astro idh-mut g2.teach: Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, WHO grade 2 — a non-enhancing, T2/FLAIR-hyperintense, often well-demarcated lesion (about 81 mL here) in a typically younger patient, frequently presenting with seizures.
mol_astro idh-mut g2.surg: Early maximal safe resection is favoured over watchful waiting, and supratotal resection beyond the FLAIR margin is actively debated as a way to delay malignant transformation. Awake mapping is the standard where the lesion approaches eloquent cortex or tracts, since these patients live long enough for any deficit to matter greatly.
mol_astro idh-mut g2.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); WHO Classification of CNS Tumours, 5th ed (2021).

mol_oligo 1p19q-codel g2.teach: Oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted, WHO grade 2 — codeletion of 1p and 19q is required for the diagnosis. Typically cortical-subcortical with indistinct margins and calcification; non-enhancing here (about 48 mL).
mol_oligo 1p19q-codel g2.surg: The most favourable glioma molecular class, with survival often measured in decades. Codeletion predicts chemosensitivity, and PCV with radiotherapy is the established adjuvant regimen. Maximal safe resection still applies, but the long survival raises the threshold for accepting any permanent deficit — a strong argument for awake mapping.
mol_oligo 1p19q-codel g2.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); WHO Classification of CNS Tumours, 5th ed (2021).

mol_astro idh-wt g3.teach: Astrocytoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 3 — histologically grade 3, but IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumours in adults often behave like glioblastoma, and molecular criteria (EGFR amplification, chromosome 7 gain with 10 loss, TERT promoter mutation) can reclassify them as such.
mol_astro idh-wt g3.surg: Treat with glioblastoma-level intent: maximal safe resection and chemoradiotherapy. Push for the full molecular profile before counselling, because the imaging and histological grade alone will underestimate the disease.
mol_astro idh-wt g3.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); WHO Classification of CNS Tumours, 5th ed (2021).

vs_tumour.teach: Vestibular schwannoma — a benign (WHO grade 1) Schwann-cell tumour of the vestibular division of CN VIII, arising at the glial-Schwann junction within the internal auditory canal and enlarging into the cerebellopontine angle. Under WHO 2021 it sits with the cranial and paraspinal nerve tumours, quite separate from the gliomas. Bilateral disease indicates NF2-related schwannomatosis. Contours here span roughly 0.2 to 7.7 mL, following the usual progression from intracanalicular, to filling the CPA, to contacting and displacing the brainstem.
vs_tumour.surg: Three management options: observation with serial imaging for small stable tumours, stereotactic radiosurgery, or microsurgical resection. Approach depends on size and residual hearing — retrosigmoid preserves the possibility of hearing and gives a wide CPA view; translabyrinthine sacrifices hearing but is a direct, brain-retraction-sparing route; middle fossa suits small intracanalicular tumours with serviceable hearing. Facial nerve preservation is the dominant operative concern, with continuous CN VII monitoring; CN V above and the lower cranial nerves below are also at risk, along with AICA and the labyrinthine artery. For large tumours, near-total resection leaving a capsule remnant on the facial nerve is often preferred to a complete resection that costs facial function.
vs_tumour.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); WHO Classification of CNS Tumours, 5th ed (2021).

vs_cochlea.teach: Cochlea, contoured alongside the tumour. Its position relative to the fundus of the internal auditory canal determines whether the labyrinth can be preserved.
vs_cochlea.surg: A critical structure for hearing preservation and for cochlear-implant candidacy. In radiosurgery, cochlear dose is a principal constraint on hearing outcome; in surgery, the translabyrinthine route deliberately sacrifices it, while retrosigmoid and middle fossa approaches aim to spare it.
vs_cochlea.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); WHO Classification of CNS Tumours, 5th ed (2021).

vs_growth.teach: The same tumour contoured at two time points, showing interval growth on serial imaging.
vs_growth.surg: Growth rate drives management. Many small vestibular schwannomas stay stable and can simply be watched; documented growth, brainstem contact or progressive hearing loss shifts the decision toward radiosurgery or resection. This is why serial volumetry, rather than a single linear diameter, is increasingly the standard.
vs_growth.ref: Youmans & Winn, Neurological Surgery (8th ed); WHO Classification of CNS Tumours, 5th ed (2021).

_spinemet.teach: Individually segmented thoracolumbar vertebrae (T7-L5) from the planning CT of a patient treated for spinal metastasis. Note that the labelled structures are the vertebral levels themselves; the metastatic deposits are not separately contoured in this dataset.
_spinemet.surg: Level-by-level anatomy underpins every spinal decision: counting levels reliably, choosing instrumented levels above and below the affected segment, and judging pedicle size and trajectory. In metastatic disease, management is guided by mechanical stability (the SINS framework), neurology (the ESCC/Bilsky grade of epidural compression) and prognosis - separation surgery with postoperative stereotactic radiotherapy has largely replaced extensive tumour debulking for most cases. Anterior vertebral-body height loss and posterior element involvement drive the instability assessment.

corticospinal tract.teach: Main descending motor pathway. Fibres arise mostly from the precentral gyrus (with contributions from premotor, supplementary motor and parietal cortex), converge through the corona radiata into the posterior limb of the internal capsule, run in the cerebral peduncle, break into bundles in the basal pons and reform as the medullary pyramids, where most fibres decussate to form the lateral corticospinal tract. Somatotopy is preserved along its course, with face fibres most anterior in the capsule.
corticospinal tract.surg: The limiting structure for most peri-rolandic, insular and deep gliomas. Subcortical monopolar stimulation with motor evoked potentials is used during resection: the stimulation threshold falls as the tract is approached and is used as a rough distance guide. Tractography shows its course preoperatively but can shift with brain shift and oedema, so it supplements rather than replaces mapping.

anterior thalamic radiation.teach: Reciprocal fibres between the anterior and medial (mediodorsal) thalamic nuclei and prefrontal and cingulate cortex, running through the anterior limb of the internal capsule. Part of the circuits supporting executive function, memory and affect.
anterior thalamic radiation.surg: Crossed by deep frontal and caudate-head approaches and lies in the anterior limb targeted in some psychiatric deep brain stimulation work. Injury is not motor-eloquent but contributes to dysexecutive and apathy syndromes after deep frontal surgery.

cingulum.teach: Long association bundle running in the white matter of the cingulate gyrus, arching from the subcallosal region around the corpus callosum and down into the parahippocampal gyrus. It links cingulate, medial frontal, parietal and medial temporal cortex and is a core connection of the limbic system and default-mode network.
cingulum.surg: Encountered in interhemispheric, trans-cingulate and medial frontal/parietal approaches. Unilateral division is usually tolerated clinically; the anterior cingulum was the historical target of cingulotomy.

cingulum (hippocampus).teach: Parahippocampal (ventral) segment of the cingulum, running in the parahippocampal gyrus from the retrosplenial region towards the medial temporal lobe. It connects posterior cingulate and precuneus with parahippocampal and entorhinal cortex, supporting memory and spatial navigation.
cingulum (hippocampus).surg: At risk in mesial temporal and posterior parahippocampal resections and in approaches through the collateral sulcus; relevant to memory outcome after dominant mesial temporal surgery.

forceps major.teach: Occipital radiation of the corpus callosum: fibres crossing in the splenium and fanning back into both occipital lobes, linking homologous visual and parieto-occipital cortex.
forceps major.surg: Splenial lesions and posterior callosotomy can disconnect the two visual hemifields; combined with a left occipital lesion this gives the classic pure alexia (alexia without agraphia). Relevant to posterior interhemispheric and occipital transtentorial approaches to the pineal region.

forceps minor.teach: Frontal radiation of the corpus callosum: fibres crossing in the genu and rostrum and curving forwards to connect the two frontal poles and orbitofrontal/medial prefrontal cortex.
forceps minor.surg: Anterior transcallosal routes to the lateral and third ventricles open the body of the callosum behind the genu to limit disconnection. Bifrontal (butterfly) gliomas spread across this path.

inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus.teach: Long ventral association bundle from occipital, posterior temporal and parietal cortex to the inferior frontal and orbitofrontal lobes. Anteriorly it narrows to pass through the temporal stem and the extreme/external capsule beneath the insula.
inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus.surg: In the dominant hemisphere it is a key tract of the ventral semantic stream: subcortical stimulation typically produces semantic paraphasias. It is the deep limit of many insular, temporal stem and posterior temporal resections and is monitored with picture naming during awake surgery.

inferior longitudinal fasciculus.teach: Ventral association bundle running along the lateral wall of the temporal horn from occipital cortex to the anterior temporal lobe, linking visual areas with temporal regions involved in object, face and word recognition.
inferior longitudinal fasciculus.surg: Relevant to posterior temporal and basal temporo-occipital resections; stimulation can produce visual naming or reading errors in the dominant hemisphere. Its function overlaps with, and may be compensated by, parallel ventral pathways.

superior longitudinal fasciculus.teach: Lateral fronto-parietal association system above the sylvian fissure, conventionally split into dorsal, middle and ventral components (SLF I-III), with the arcuate fasciculus curving round the end of the sylvian fissure into the temporal lobe. It connects premotor and prefrontal cortex with parietal association areas.
superior longitudinal fasciculus.surg: Dominant side: the ventral components and arcuate support phonological processing and articulation, and stimulation produces phonemic paraphasias or speech arrest. Non-dominant side: it supports visuospatial attention, and injury can cause neglect, so line-bisection tasks are used during awake right-sided surgery.

superior longitudinal fasciculus (tempor.teach: The temporal projection of the SLF system, largely corresponding to the arcuate fasciculus: it arches around the posterior end of the sylvian fissure to link posterior temporal cortex with parietal and frontal (Broca/ventral premotor) regions.
superior longitudinal fasciculus (tempor.surg: In the dominant hemisphere, damage classically produces conduction-type aphasia with poor repetition, and stimulation elicits phonemic paraphasias. It is the deep limit of posterior superior temporal and supramarginal resections.

uncinate fasciculus.teach: Hook-shaped bundle joining the temporal pole, anterior temporal lobe and amygdala region with orbitofrontal cortex, passing through the temporal stem at the limen insulae.
uncinate fasciculus.surg: Divided in anterior temporal lobectomy and in many insular and fronto-orbital resections. Reported deficits after resection are often subtle or transient; its role in semantic memory, naming of proper nouns and socio-emotional behaviour is still debated.

acoustic radiation.teach: Thalamocortical auditory projection from the medial geniculate body to the transverse temporal (Heschl) gyrus, running horizontally below the lentiform nucleus through the sublenticular internal capsule.
acoustic radiation.surg: Because hearing is represented bilaterally, unilateral injury rarely causes clinical deafness, but it is crossed by trans-sylvian and superior temporal approaches.

optic radiation.teach: Geniculocalcarine pathway from the lateral geniculate body to the calcarine cortex. Ventral fibres (serving the upper contralateral quadrant) loop forwards over the roof of the temporal horn as Meyer's loop before turning back; dorsal fibres run directly in the lateral wall of the atrium and occipital horn.
optic radiation.surg: Anterior temporal lobectomy and transcortical temporal approaches risk a contralateral superior quadrantanopia; the anterior extent of Meyer's loop varies considerably between people, so tractography is used for planning. Lateral approaches to the atrium risk a homonymous hemianopia, which is one reason trans-sulcal or superior parietal routes are sometimes preferred.

callosal body.teach: The corpus callosum: the largest commissure, linking homologous cortex of the two hemispheres. It is divided from front to back into rostrum, genu, body and splenium, and forms the roof of the lateral ventricles.
callosal body.surg: The anterior interhemispheric transcallosal approach uses a short callosotomy in the body to reach the lateral and third ventricles. Longer divisions, or division of the splenium, increase the risk of disconnection syndromes. Corpus callosotomy is also a palliative operation for drop attacks.

fornix.teach: Main output of the hippocampus: fibres collect as the fimbria, form the crus under the splenium, join as the body under the corpus callosum and descend as the columns in front of the foramen of Monro to reach the mammillary bodies and septal region. It is part of the Papez circuit.
fornix.surg: The column forms the anterosuperior margin of the foramen of Monro and is at risk in transforaminal, transchoroidal and interforniceal approaches to the third ventricle. Bilateral injury can produce a severe, lasting anterograde amnesia.

superior occipito-frontal fascicle.teach: A probabilistic label in the Julich atlas for a putative bundle running dorsolateral to the lateral ventricle between frontal and parietal-occipital regions. Whether a distinct superior fronto-occipital fasciculus exists in humans is disputed; some dissection studies interpret it as part of the subcallosal/striatal fibre systems.
superior occipito-frontal fascicle.surg: Treat as a label rather than a mapped functional tract; there is no established intraoperative stimulation response attributed to it.

aca territory.teach: Territory of the anterior cerebral artery cortical branches: the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes back to the parieto-occipital sulcus, a strip of the superior convexity, and most of the corpus callosum. It includes the medial motor and sensory leg area on the paracentral lobule.
aca territory.surg: Occlusion gives contralateral leg-predominant weakness, and abulia if bilateral. Surgically relevant to anterior communicating aneurysms, interhemispheric approaches (pericallosal and callosomarginal arteries lie on the corpus callosum and in the cingulate sulcus) and falcine meningiomas.

medial lenticulostriate territory.teach: Deep territory of the medial lenticulostriate perforators arising from A1 and the proximal anterior cerebral artery, including the recurrent artery of Heubner. It covers the head of the caudate, anterior limb of the internal capsule and anteromedial lentiform nucleus.
medial lenticulostriate territory.surg: These perforators, and Heubner's artery in particular, must be protected during anterior communicating complex aneurysm dissection and subfrontal approaches; injury can cause face-arm weakness and, in the dominant hemisphere, language disturbance.

lateral lenticulostriate territory.teach: Deep territory of the lateral lenticulostriate arteries arising from the M1 segment (and sometimes early M2). It supplies the putamen, lateral globus pallidus, upper internal capsule and adjacent corona radiata.
lateral lenticulostriate territory.surg: The most lateral lenticulostriate artery marks the medial limit of resection in insular glioma surgery; injury gives a capsular infarct with dense contralateral hemiplegia. These end-arteries are also the classic source of hypertensive putaminal haemorrhage.

mca cortical territory.teach: Cortical territory of the middle cerebral artery branches, divided in this atlas into frontal, parietal, temporal, occipital and insular parts. The MCA supplies most of the lateral convexity, including the face-arm motor and sensory cortex, and in the dominant hemisphere the perisylvian language network.
mca cortical territory.surg: Relevant to MCA bifurcation aneurysms, trans-sylvian approaches and cortical branch preservation during convexity and insular resections. Sacrificing an en-passage cortical branch can infarct eloquent cortex downstream of the resection.

mca insular territory.teach: Insular part of the MCA territory, supplied by M2 branches running over the insula and their short insular perforators, which reach the extreme and external capsules and claustrum.
mca insular territory.surg: In insular surgery the M2 trunks are skeletonised and preserved; the long insular perforators from the posterior insula can reach the corona radiata and corticospinal tract, so they limit resection in the upper posterior insula.

pca temporal territory.teach: Temporal part of the posterior cerebral artery territory: inferior temporal branches supplying the inferomedial temporal lobe, including the hippocampus, parahippocampal and fusiform gyri.
pca temporal territory.surg: Relevant to mesial temporal surgery and subtemporal approaches, where P2 and its temporal branches run in the ambient cistern. Bilateral ischaemia here can impair memory.

pca occipital territory.teach: Occipital part of the posterior cerebral artery territory, supplied by the calcarine and parieto-occipital branches. It includes the primary visual cortex around the calcarine sulcus.
pca occipital territory.surg: Occlusion typically gives a contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing because the occipital pole may also receive MCA collaterals. Relevant to occipital approaches and to PCA sacrifice during treatment of posterior circulation lesions.

posterior choroidal and thalamoperforato.teach: Deep posterior-circulation territory: thalamoperforating arteries from P1 and the posterior communicating artery, thalamogeniculate arteries from P2, and the medial and lateral posterior choroidal arteries. It covers much of the thalamus, parts of the midbrain and the choroid plexus of the third and lateral ventricles.
posterior choroidal and thalamoperforato.surg: These perforators must be preserved in basilar apex and P1 aneurysm surgery and in pineal and thalamic approaches. A single dominant thalamoperforator (the artery of Percheron) can supply both paramedian thalami.

anterior choroidal and thalamoperforator.teach: Territory of the anterior choroidal artery (from the supraclinoid ICA) with neighbouring thalamoperforators: optic tract, lower posterior limb of the internal capsule, lateral geniculate body, medial temporal structures (uncus, amygdala, anterior hippocampus) and choroid plexus of the temporal horn.
anterior choroidal and thalamoperforator.surg: Injury can produce hemiparesis, hemisensory loss and hemianopia. The artery must be identified in posterior communicating and anterior choroidal aneurysm surgery and during mesial temporal resection, where it enters the temporal horn at the choroidal fissure.

basilar perforator territory.teach: Territory of the paramedian and short circumferential perforators from the basilar artery, supplying the pons and parts of the midbrain. The atlas labels it separately for left and right of the midline.
basilar perforator territory.surg: Perforator injury during basilar trunk and apex surgery or endovascular treatment can cause brainstem infarction; this is a main reason these aneurysms are high risk.

superior cerebellar artery territory.teach: Territory of the superior cerebellar artery: the superior (tentorial) surface of the cerebellum, much of the dentate nucleus, the superior cerebellar peduncle and parts of the upper pons and midbrain tegmentum.
superior cerebellar artery territory.surg: Its branches are the commonest offending vessel in trigeminal neuralgia microvascular decompression, and the artery is encountered in supracerebellar infratentorial and subtemporal approaches.

inferior cerebellar territory.teach: Combined territory of the anterior and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries: the petrosal and suboccipital surfaces of the cerebellum, the tonsils and inferior vermis, and (for PICA) the lateral medulla.
inferior cerebellar territory.surg: PICA occlusion is the classic cause of lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome. AICA and its labyrinthine branches lie in the cerebellopontine angle in vestibular schwannoma and microvascular decompression surgery; PICA loops are met in far-lateral and suboccipital approaches.

lateral ventricle (territory atlas).teach: The lateral ventricle is included as a separate label in this territory atlas, so it is not assigned to an arterial territory. Its choroid plexus is supplied by the anterior and posterior choroidal arteries.

subclavian artery.teach: On the right it arises from the brachiocephalic trunk and on the left directly from the aortic arch. It arches over the pleural dome behind scalenus anterior and gives the vertebral artery as its first branch, plus the thyrocervical and costocervical trunks and the internal thoracic artery.
subclavian artery.surg: Relevant to vertebral artery origin disease, subclavian steal and anterior cervical exposures low in the neck; the vertebral artery origin is the usual approach route for posterior circulation endovascular access.

external carotid.teach: Branch of the common carotid at the carotid bifurcation (usually near C3-C4). It supplies the face, scalp, dura and neck through its branches, including the superior thyroid, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, superficial temporal and maxillary arteries; the middle meningeal artery comes from the maxillary artery.
external carotid.surg: Its branches supply most meningiomas and dural arteriovenous fistulas and are targets for preoperative embolisation. The superficial temporal and occipital arteries are donors for extracranial-intracranial bypass, so scalp incisions can be planned to preserve them.

subclavian vein.teach: Continuation of the axillary vein, running in front of scalenus anterior and behind the clavicle to join the internal jugular vein and form the brachiocephalic vein.
subclavian vein.surg: Common site for central venous access and a landmark for the distal end of ventriculoatrial shunt catheters (placed via the internal jugular route into the right atrium).

brachiocephalic trunk.teach: First and largest branch of the aortic arch, dividing behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right subclavian and right common carotid arteries.
brachiocephalic trunk.surg: Relevant to catheter access to the right carotid and vertebral circulation and to low anterior cervical/cervicothoracic exposures.

superior vena cava.teach: Formed by the union of the two brachiocephalic veins behind the right first costal cartilage; it drains the head, neck and upper limbs into the right atrium.
superior vena cava.surg: The target zone for the distal catheter tip in ventriculoatrial shunting is at or near the junction of the superior vena cava with the right atrium.

thyroid gland.teach: Two lobes joined by an isthmus lying over the second to fourth tracheal rings, enclosed in pretracheal fascia. The recurrent laryngeal nerves run close to its posterior surface in the tracheo-oesophageal groove.
thyroid gland.surg: Retracted medially with the trachea and oesophagus during the anterior (Smith-Robinson) approach to the cervical spine. The superior and inferior thyroid arteries may cross the field at upper and lower levels respectively.

thyroid cartilage.teach: Largest laryngeal cartilage, forming the laryngeal prominence. Its upper border lies at about C4 and it is a standard surface landmark for level selection in anterior cervical surgery.
thyroid cartilage.surg: Palpable landmarks help place the skin incision for anterior cervical approaches: hyoid about C3, thyroid cartilage about C4-C5, cricoid about C6. These are approximate and are confirmed with fluoroscopy.

cricoid cartilage.teach: Complete ring of cartilage at the lower larynx, usually at the level of C6. The inferior thyroid artery and the recurrent laryngeal nerve entering the larynx are nearby.
cricoid cartilage.surg: Commonly used surface landmark for the C6 level in anterior cervical approaches; C6 also carries the prominent anterior (carotid, Chassaignac) tubercle.

hyoid.teach: U-shaped bone suspended by muscles and ligaments at about the level of C3, anchoring the tongue above and the infrahyoid strap muscles below.
hyoid.surg: Surface landmark for the C3 level; high anterior cervical approaches (C2-C3) work above or around it, with the hypoglossal and superior laryngeal nerves at risk.

cervical vertebra (h&n).teach: Typical cervical vertebrae (C3-C6) have a small body with uncinate processes, foramina transversaria carrying the vertebral artery (usually from C6 upwards) and bifid spinous processes. C7 (vertebra prominens) has a long spinous process and a foramen transversarium that normally transmits only veins.
cervical vertebra (h&n).surg: Anterior approaches (discectomy, corpectomy, arthroplasty) and posterior approaches (laminoplasty, laminectomy with lateral mass screws) are the workhorses of cervical surgery. The vertebral artery lies just lateral to the uncovertebral joint, which limits lateral decompression.

thoracic vertebra (h&n).teach: Upper thoracic vertebrae have heart-shaped bodies, costal facets for rib articulation and long, downward-sloping spinous processes. The canal is relatively narrow compared with the cord.
thoracic vertebra (h&n).surg: The cervicothoracic junction is hard to image and reach anteriorly (sternum, great vessels); posterior pedicle screw fixation is standard. The rib head and costovertebral joint are landmarks for level counting and for costotransversectomy approaches.

atlas (h&n).teach: First cervical vertebra (C1): a ring with no body, anterior and posterior arches and two lateral masses that articulate with the occipital condyles above and the axis below.
atlas (h&n).surg: The vertebral artery runs in a groove on the upper surface of the posterior arch, which limits lateral subperiosteal dissection along the arch in posterior craniocervical exposures; the safe distance from the midline varies between patients and is checked on the preoperative CT.

axis (h&n).teach: Second cervical vertebra (C2), carrying the odontoid process (dens) around which the atlas rotates. It has large pars interarticularis and a bifid spinous process.
axis (h&n).surg: Common fracture site (odontoid and hangman fractures). C2 pars, pedicle or translaminar screws are the anchor points for upper cervical fixation; the vertebral artery course must be checked on CT first.

clavicle.teach: S-shaped bone linking the sternum to the acromion, overlying the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus.
clavicle.surg: Landmark for supraclavicular exposures of the brachial plexus and lower neck.

sternum.teach: Manubrium, body and xiphoid process. The manubrium lies in front of the great vessels and the upper thoracic vertebrae.
sternum.surg: The manubrium blocks direct anterior access to the upper thoracic spine; low cervical/upper thoracic anterior approaches may need a manubriotomy or sternotomy. Sternal level is judged against the upper thoracic bodies on sagittal imaging.

rib.teach: Upper ribs articulate with the vertebral bodies and transverse processes at the costovertebral and costotransverse joints.
rib.surg: Counting ribs on imaging is a standard cross-check of thoracic level. The rib head is removed in costotransversectomy and lateral extracavitary approaches to reach the ventral thoracic canal.

parotid gland.teach: Largest salivary gland, wrapped around the ramus of the mandible in front of the ear. The facial nerve runs through it after leaving the stylomastoid foramen, dividing the gland into superficial and deep parts.
parotid gland.surg: Pre-auricular skin incisions for pterional and zygomatic approaches stay close to the tragus and above the zygomatic arch to avoid the facial nerve branches and parotid.

temporalis.teach: Fan-shaped muscle from the temporal fossa, passing under the zygomatic arch to the coronoid process of the mandible; it elevates and retracts the mandible. It is covered by the temporalis fascia, which splits into two layers above the arch.
temporalis.surg: Reflected in pterional, frontotemporal and orbitozygomatic craniotomies. Interfascial or subfascial dissection protects the frontal branch of the facial nerve, which runs in the superficial fat pad above the arch. Careful handling limits postoperative temporal hollowing; the muscle is also a vascularised flap for skull-base repair.

trapezius.teach: Large flat muscle from the occiput and spinous processes to the clavicle and scapula. It is supplied by the accessory nerve (CN XI).
trapezius.surg: Split or detached in midline posterior cervical and suboccipital exposures. The accessory nerve in the posterior triangle is at risk in lateral neck dissection.

masseter.teach: Thick muscle from the zygomatic arch to the lateral surface of the mandibular ramus and angle; the main elevator of the mandible. It is supplied by the masseteric branch of the mandibular nerve (V3).
masseter.surg: The masseteric nerve is a donor for facial reanimation (masseteric-to-facial nerve transfer). The muscle is displaced with the zygomatic arch in zygomatic and orbitozygomatic approaches.

levator scapulae.teach: Runs from the transverse processes of C1-C4 to the upper medial border of the scapula; it elevates the scapula.
levator scapulae.surg: A lateral landmark in posterior cervical and far-lateral exposures, with the vertebral artery and suboccipital triangle deep to it.

scalene muscles.teach: Scalenus anterior, medius and posterior run from the cervical transverse processes to the first and second ribs. The brachial plexus roots and the subclavian artery pass between anterior and middle scalene; the phrenic nerve lies on scalenus anterior.
scalene muscles.surg: Key landmarks in supraclavicular brachial plexus exploration and in anterolateral approaches to the cervical spine and vertebral artery.

sternocleidomastoid.teach: Runs from the sternum and clavicle to the mastoid process and superior nuchal line, supplied by the accessory nerve. It divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles.
sternocleidomastoid.surg: The anterior cervical approach develops the plane medial to it and to the carotid sheath. Its mastoid attachment is detached in far-lateral and retrosigmoid exposures, and the muscle is a landmark for the accessory nerve.

zygomatic muscle.teach: Zygomaticus major and minor run from the zygomatic bone to the corner of the mouth and upper lip and are muscles of facial expression, supplied by zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve.
zygomatic muscle.surg: Not usually part of cranial exposures, but a reference for facial nerve branch function in facial reanimation surgery.

precentral gyrus.teach: Primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4) lies mainly on the anterior bank of the central sulcus and the precentral gyrus. It is somatotopically organised as the motor homunculus: leg medially on the paracentral lobule, then trunk, arm and hand (the hand knob), with face and tongue lowest near the sylvian fissure.
precentral gyrus.surg: The central sulcus is identified before resection (hand knob on axial MRI, phase reversal of somatosensory evoked potentials, direct stimulation). Lesions here are resected with cortical and subcortical motor mapping; the precentral gyrus itself is usually preserved.

postcentral gyrus.teach: Primary somatosensory cortex (areas 3a, 3b, 1 and 2) runs from the posterior bank of the central sulcus over the postcentral gyrus, with a sensory homunculus mirroring the motor one.
postcentral gyrus.surg: SSEP phase reversal across the central sulcus confirms its position. Resection of the postcentral gyrus can cause lasting proprioceptive loss and clumsiness even with preserved strength, so it is treated as eloquent.

superior frontal gyrus.teach: Runs along the upper medial frontal lobe from the frontal pole to the precentral sulcus. Its posterior part contains the supplementary motor area (SMA) and pre-SMA medially, and its anterior part is prefrontal association cortex.
superior frontal gyrus.surg: Posterior resections can cause SMA syndrome: contralateral akinesia and, on the dominant side, reduced speech initiation. It usually recovers over weeks to months but must be discussed during consent. The frontal aslant tract runs from here to the inferior frontal gyrus.

middle frontal gyrus.teach: Lies between the superior and inferior frontal sulci. Its posterior part includes premotor cortex and the frontal eye field region, and its anterior part is dorsolateral prefrontal cortex involved in working memory and executive control.
middle frontal gyrus.surg: The posterior middle frontal gyrus borders premotor and hand motor territory, and in some people speech-related sites are found here on mapping. The anterior part is often a safe corridor for transcortical access to the frontal horn.

inferior frontal gyrus.teach: Divided by the rami of the sylvian fissure into opercular (area 44), triangular (area 45) and orbital (area 47) parts. In the dominant hemisphere the opercular and triangular parts form classical Broca's area.
inferior frontal gyrus.surg: Awake mapping is used for dominant-side lesions because language sites vary between people and do not always match the classical boundaries. The pars triangularis is also a trans-opercular route to the anterior insula.

frontal pole.teach: Most anterior part of the frontal lobe (frontopolar area 10), involved in higher-order planning and integrating multiple goals.
frontal pole.surg: Frontal pole resection is generally well tolerated neurologically, though subtle executive or behavioural change can follow. The frontal sinus lies in front of it in anterior craniotomies.

orbitofrontal gyri.teach: Orbital surface of the frontal lobe, including the straight gyrus (gyrus rectus) medially and the medial, anterior, posterior and lateral orbital gyri around the H-shaped orbital sulcus. It sits on the orbital roof and supports reward valuation, decision making and social behaviour.
orbitofrontal gyri.surg: Gyrus rectus is partially resected in some approaches to anterior communicating aneurysms. The olfactory tract runs in the olfactory sulcus lateral to it and is at risk with subfrontal retraction. Orbitofrontal injury can produce disinhibition and personality change.

paracentral lobule.teach: Medial continuation of the precentral and postcentral gyri around the upper end of the central sulcus, containing the motor and sensory representation of the contralateral leg and foot. It also has a role in bladder control.
paracentral lobule.surg: Parasagittal and falcine meningiomas and interhemispheric approaches put it at risk, especially through injury to draining veins into the superior sagittal sinus, which can cause venous infarction and leg weakness.

cingulate gyrus.teach: Arches around the corpus callosum above the callosal sulcus. The anterior cingulate is involved in motivation, error monitoring and autonomic control; the posterior cingulate and isthmus are hubs of the default-mode network and continue into the parahippocampal gyrus.
cingulate gyrus.surg: Traversed or retracted in interhemispheric transcallosal approaches. Bilateral anterior cingulate injury can cause akinetic mutism; unilateral resection is usually tolerated. The cingulate motor areas lie in the cingulate sulcus behind the SMA.

parahippocampal gyrus.teach: Medial temporal gyrus below the hippocampus, bounded laterally by the collateral sulcus. Anteriorly it hooks back as the uncus and contains entorhinal cortex; posteriorly it holds parahippocampal cortex involved in scene processing and navigation.
parahippocampal gyrus.surg: Resected in selective amygdalohippocampectomy and mesial temporal tumour surgery. The posterior cerebral artery and the ambient cistern lie medial to it, and the trochlear nerve runs at the tentorial edge nearby.

ambiens gyrus.teach: Small medial temporal gyrus on the uncus, part of the anterior parahippocampal region overlying the amygdala and entorhinal cortex, facing the ambient cistern.
ambiens gyrus.surg: At the medial edge of mesial temporal resections, next to the posterior cerebral artery, oculomotor nerve and cerebral peduncle; subpial technique protects these.

hippocampus.teach: Curved grey matter structure in the floor and medial wall of the temporal horn (cornu ammonis fields and dentate gyrus), continuous with the subiculum and entorhinal cortex. It is essential for forming new declarative memories; the dominant side is more involved in verbal memory.
hippocampus.surg: Hippocampal sclerosis is the commonest substrate of drug-resistant mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, treated by anterior temporal lobectomy or selective amygdalohippocampectomy. Resection on the dominant side, particularly with a normal-looking hippocampus, carries a risk of verbal memory decline.

amygdala.teach: Nuclear complex in the dorsomedial temporal lobe in front of the temporal horn and hippocampal head, with laterobasal, centromedial and superficial groups. It is central to emotional learning, threat processing and autonomic responses.
amygdala.surg: Removed with the hippocampus in mesial temporal epilepsy surgery. Its upper boundary is not visible, so resection is guided by landmarks such as the M1 segment and the level of the optic tract to avoid entering the globus pallidus and basal forebrain.

insula.teach: Cortex hidden deep in the sylvian fissure, covered by the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula and bounded by the circular (peri-insular) sulcus. The central insular sulcus divides it into anterior short gyri and posterior long gyri. It integrates interoceptive, visceral, taste, pain and emotional information, and the anterior insula also contributes to speech.
insula.surg: Insular gliomas are resected by trans-sylvian or trans-opercular (trans-cortical) routes. Limits are the M2 branches and long insular perforators superiorly and posteriorly, the lateral lenticulostriate arteries medially, and the corticospinal tract in the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

limen insulae.teach: Threshold of the insula at its anteroinferior apex, where the insula meets the orbitofrontal surface and the temporal pole. The M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery turns (genu) here into M2.
limen insulae.surg: A key landmark in trans-sylvian dissection and insular surgery. The uncinate and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculi pass through the temporal stem just beneath it.

claustrum.teach: Thin sheet of grey matter between the insula and putamen, separated by the extreme capsule laterally and the external capsule medially. It has widespread reciprocal cortical connections and its function is still under investigation.
claustrum.surg: Lies at the deep limit of insular resections; the external capsule and claustrum mark the approach towards the lateral lenticulostriate territory.

superior temporal gyrus.teach: Upper temporal gyrus, bounded by the sylvian fissure above and the superior temporal sulcus below. Its upper surface (planum temporale behind Heschl's gyrus) and posterior part in the dominant hemisphere form Wernicke's receptive language region; the anterior part lies near the temporal pole.
superior temporal gyrus.surg: Dominant posterior superior temporal resections carry a risk of receptive aphasia and are mapped awake. In the non-dominant hemisphere it is more commonly used for access to the temporal horn and insula.

middle temporal gyrus.teach: Between the superior and inferior temporal sulci. The anterior part is involved in semantic processing; the posterior part near the occipital lobe includes motion-sensitive visual cortex (MT/V5 region).
middle temporal gyrus.surg: The standard corticotomy route into the temporal horn in the non-dominant hemisphere. In the dominant hemisphere, naming sites are often found here, so posterior resections are mapped.

inferior temporal gyrus.teach: Lateral inferior temporal gyrus continuing onto the basal surface. It forms part of the ventral visual stream for object recognition and, on the dominant side, contributes to naming.
inferior temporal gyrus.surg: Basal temporal language areas have been described on the dominant inferior temporal and fusiform gyri, so posterior basal resections can affect naming. Subtemporal approaches retract this surface; the vein of Labbé drains across it.

fusiform gyrus.teach: Basal occipitotemporal gyrus between the collateral and occipitotemporal sulci. It contains face-selective cortex (fusiform face area) and, on the dominant side, the visual word form area.
fusiform gyrus.surg: Injury can cause prosopagnosia (bilateral or right-sided) and pure alexia (left-sided). Relevant to basal temporal and occipitotemporal resections and to epilepsy surgery with subdural or stereo-EEG mapping.

temporal pole.teach: Most anterior tip of the temporal lobe, in the middle cranial fossa behind the greater wing of the sphenoid. It is association cortex linked to semantic and social-emotional processing, with strong connections to the orbitofrontal cortex through the uncinate fasciculus.
temporal pole.surg: Resected as part of standard anterior temporal lobectomy. Its extent is often measured from the tip, but the safe length differs between dominant and non-dominant sides, and language mapping or tailored resection is used on the dominant side.

transverse temporal gyrus.teach: Heschl's gyrus: runs obliquely across the upper surface of the superior temporal gyrus into the sylvian fissure and contains primary auditory cortex (A1). Its tonotopic map runs roughly from low to high frequencies along its length.
transverse temporal gyrus.surg: Unilateral injury rarely gives clinical hearing loss because of bilateral representation, but it is a landmark in trans-sylvian dissection and marks the front of the planum temporale.

superior parietal lobule.teach: Above the intraparietal sulcus, behind the postcentral gyrus. It integrates somatosensory and visual information for reaching, grasping and spatial attention (dorsal stream).
superior parietal lobule.surg: The superior parietal transcortical approach is a common route to the atrium of the lateral ventricle because it avoids language cortex and much of the optic radiation. Injury can cause optic ataxia or contralateral sensory-motor neglect.

inferior parietal lobule.teach: Below the intraparietal sulcus, comprising the supramarginal gyrus around the end of the sylvian fissure and the angular gyrus around the end of the superior temporal sulcus. It is a multimodal association region for language, praxis, calculation and spatial attention.
inferior parietal lobule.surg: Dominant-side injury can produce conduction aphasia, alexia with agraphia or Gerstmann features; non-dominant injury typically causes neglect. Lesions here are mapped awake.

supramarginal gyrus.teach: Anterior part of the inferior parietal lobule, capping the posterior end of the sylvian fissure. On the dominant side it is involved in phonological processing and praxis; the arcuate/SLF system runs beneath it.
supramarginal gyrus.surg: Awake mapping commonly finds phonological and repetition sites here on the dominant side; subcortical stimulation of the underlying arcuate fasciculus produces phonemic paraphasias.

precuneus.teach: Medial parietal cortex between the paracentral lobule and the parieto-occipital sulcus. A hub of the default-mode network, involved in self-referential thought, memory retrieval and visuospatial imagery.
precuneus.surg: Traversed in posterior interhemispheric approaches to the atrium, splenium and pineal region. Unilateral resection is generally well tolerated.

cuneus.teach: Wedge of medial occipital cortex between the parieto-occipital and calcarine sulci. Its cortex along the upper bank of the calcarine sulcus represents the contralateral lower visual quadrant.
cuneus.surg: Occipital interhemispheric approaches retract it; injury gives a contralateral inferior quadrantanopia.

lingual gyrus.teach: Medial occipital gyrus below the calcarine sulcus. Its upper edge along the calcarine sulcus represents the contralateral upper visual quadrant; more anteriorly it contributes to colour and scene processing.
lingual gyrus.surg: Injury gives a contralateral superior quadrantanopia, and bilateral damage can cause achromatopsia (loss of colour vision). Relevant to occipital and posterior basal temporal approaches.

lateral occipital gyrus.teach: Lateral surface of the occipital lobe, containing higher visual areas involved in object shape (lateral occipital complex) and, towards the temporo-occipital junction, motion.
lateral occipital gyrus.surg: Lateral occipital resections may spare the primary visual cortex but can damage optic radiation fibres heading to the calcarine cortex; field testing and tractography help planning.

visual cortex.teach: Primary visual cortex (V1, striate cortex, Brodmann area 17) lines the calcarine sulcus on the medial occipital surface and extends onto the occipital pole, which represents the central (macular) field.
visual cortex.surg: Injury gives a contralateral homonymous field defect. Occipital lobe surgery is planned with visual fields and tractography; a posterior-pole defect affects central vision, while anterior calcarine injury affects the peripheral field.

central sulcus.teach: Separates the precentral (motor) and postcentral (sensory) gyri. It usually runs continuously from the superior border to near the sylvian fissure without joining it, with a posteriorly convex hand knob in its upper-middle portion.
central sulcus.surg: Identifying it is the first step in peri-rolandic surgery: MRI signs (hand knob, pars marginalis of the cingulate sulcus), SSEP phase reversal and direct stimulation are combined.

sulcus (landmark).teach: Cortical sulcus included in this atlas as a landmark. Sulci bound gyri and functional areas, carry arterial branches and veins, and form natural corridors to deeper structures.
sulcus (landmark).surg: Trans-sulcal routes open a sulcus to reach subcortical lesions with less cortical transection than a transgyral route, but the arteries within the sulcus must be preserved. Recognising sulcal patterns on MRI and at surgery is key to orientation.

calcarine sulcus.teach: Deep medial occipital sulcus lined by primary visual cortex; its upper bank represents the lower visual field and its lower bank the upper field. Anteriorly it joins the parieto-occipital sulcus.
calcarine sulcus.surg: Landmark for occipital interhemispheric approaches and for estimating the risk of field defects.

intraparietal sulcus.teach: Separates the superior from the inferior parietal lobule, running back from the postcentral sulcus. Its banks contain areas for eye movements, reaching and grasping.
intraparietal sulcus.surg: A common trans-sulcal corridor to deep parietal and atrial lesions.

caudate nucleus.teach: C-shaped nucleus with head, body and tail following the lateral wall of the lateral ventricle. With the putamen it forms the striatum, receiving cortical input for motor, cognitive and limbic loops.
caudate nucleus.surg: The caudate head forms the lateral wall of the frontal horn, a landmark in endoscopic and transcallosal ventricular surgery; the thalamostriate vein runs in the groove between caudate and thalamus to the foramen of Monro.

putamen.teach: Lateral part of the lentiform nucleus, separated from the claustrum by the external capsule and from the globus pallidus by the lateral medullary lamina. Part of the striatum.
putamen.surg: The commonest site of hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage (from lateral lenticulostriate arteries). It lies at the deep limit of insular resections.

globus pallidus.teach: Medial part of the lentiform nucleus, divided into external (GPe) and internal (GPi) segments. GPi is a main output nucleus of the basal ganglia to the thalamus.
globus pallidus.surg: GPi is a standard deep brain stimulation target for dystonia and Parkinson's disease; the optic tract lies just below its ventral border and the internal capsule medially and posteriorly, which accounts for visual and capsular side effects of stimulation.

nucleus accumbens.teach: Ventral striatum where the caudate head and putamen meet below the anterior limb of the internal capsule. Central to reward and motivation.
nucleus accumbens.surg: Investigated as a target for deep brain stimulation in psychiatric disorders (research setting).

subthalamic nucleus.teach: Small lens-shaped nucleus below the thalamus and above the substantia nigra, part of the indirect basal ganglia pathway.
subthalamic nucleus.surg: The most common deep brain stimulation target for Parkinson's disease. The dorsolateral motor part is targeted; spread of current to the internal capsule, oculomotor fibres or medial limbic territory explains many stimulation side effects.

substantia nigra.teach: Midbrain nucleus dorsal to the cerebral peduncle: pars compacta (dopaminergic neurons projecting to the striatum) and pars reticulata (GABAergic output similar to GPi).
substantia nigra.surg: Degeneration of the pars compacta causes Parkinson's disease. It lies just below the subthalamic nucleus on the typical DBS trajectory.

red nucleus.teach: Rounded midbrain nucleus in the tegmentum at the level of the superior colliculus, receiving dentate output through the superior cerebellar peduncle.
red nucleus.surg: Useful MRI landmark for subthalamic nucleus targeting (the STN lies anterolateral to it). Lesions in its region can cause tremor and oculomotor palsy (Benedikt syndrome).

ventral tegmental area.teach: Midline dopaminergic cell group in the midbrain tegmentum medial to the substantia nigra, projecting to limbic and prefrontal targets (mesolimbic and mesocortical pathways).
ventral tegmental area.surg: Relevant to reward circuitry and to side effects of stimulation near the medial subthalamic region.

basal forebrain.teach: Grey matter below the anterior commissure and globus pallidus, including the nucleus basalis of Meynert (major cholinergic source for the cortex) and the septal nuclei.
basal forebrain.surg: The basal forebrain can be injured by anterior communicating complex aneurysm rupture or surgery (perforator territory), which can cause memory disturbance and confabulation.

mammillary body.teach: Paired nuclei on the floor of the third ventricle behind the tuber cinereum, receiving the fornix and projecting to the anterior thalamus via the mammillothalamic tract (Papez circuit).
mammillary body.surg: Landmark in endoscopic third ventriculostomy: the floor is opened in the midline between the mammillary bodies behind and the infundibular recess in front, with the basilar apex below.

mammillothalamic tract.teach: Bundle from the mammillary body to the anterior thalamic nucleus, part of the Papez circuit.
mammillothalamic tract.surg: Visible on high-resolution MRI; used as a landmark in anterior thalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation for epilepsy. Bilateral injury impairs memory.

pineal body.teach: Midline gland above the tectal plate in the quadrigeminal cistern, attached to the roof of the third ventricle. It produces melatonin.
pineal body.surg: Pineal-region tumours cause hydrocephalus via aqueductal compression and Parinaud syndrome via tectal compression. Approaches include the supracerebellar infratentorial, occipital transtentorial and interhemispheric routes; the deep venous system (internal cerebral veins, basal veins, vein of Galen) is closely related.

anterior commissure.teach: Small commissure crossing in the anterior wall of the third ventricle, linking the anterior temporal lobes and olfactory regions.
anterior commissure.surg: The anterior and posterior commissures (AC-PC line) are the reference frame for stereotactic targeting of deep brain nuclei.

corpus callosum.teach: Largest commissure, linking homologous cortex of the two hemispheres. It forms the roof of the lateral ventricles and is divided into rostrum, genu, body and splenium.
corpus callosum.surg: The anterior interhemispheric transcallosal approach opens a short segment of the body to reach the ventricles; longer or splenial divisions increase the risk of disconnection. Callosal involvement by glioma (butterfly pattern) usually reduces the resectable fraction.

septum pellucidum.teach: Thin double membrane between the frontal horns and bodies of the lateral ventricles, stretching from the corpus callosum to the fornix.
septum pellucidum.surg: Opened (septostomy) endoscopically when one lateral ventricle is trapped. It is a midline landmark on imaging for midline shift.

internal medullary lamina.teach: Y-shaped sheet of white matter dividing the thalamus into anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups; the intralaminar nuclei (including the centromedian nucleus) lie within it.
internal medullary lamina.surg: An anatomical landmark for thalamic nuclear targeting in functional neurosurgery.

cerebral white matter.teach: Hemispheric white matter: association, commissural and projection fibres beneath the cortex. This atlas groups it as one structure per hemisphere.
cerebral white matter.surg: All transcortical approaches cross it; knowledge of the major tracts within it (corticospinal, arcuate/SLF, IFOF, optic radiation) determines safe corridors. Turn on the MNI overlay tract layer to see them.

thalamic nucleus.teach: Thalamic nucleus. The thalamus relays and modulates almost all information reaching the cortex and is organised into anterior, medial, lateral, intralaminar and posterior (pulvinar, geniculate) groups, each with specific cortical partners.
thalamic nucleus.surg: Thalamic lesions are approached by transcallosal, transcortical-transventricular or posterior interhemispheric routes depending on which surface they reach. Individual nuclei are targets in functional neurosurgery.

ventral intermediate / ventral lateral t.teach: Motor thalamus: the ventral lateral nucleus receives cerebellar (dentatothalamic) and pallidal input and projects to motor and premotor cortex. Its posterior part corresponds to the ventral intermediate nucleus (Vim) of the Hassler nomenclature.
ventral intermediate / ventral lateral t.surg: Vim is the standard deep brain stimulation or lesioning (including focused ultrasound) target for essential tremor. The sensory relay nucleus (VPL/VPM) lies just behind it, so paraesthesia during stimulation indicates a posterior electrode position.

ventral posterior thalamus.teach: Main somatosensory relay: the ventral posterolateral nucleus (VPL) receives the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract from the body, and the ventral posteromedial nucleus (VPM) receives trigeminal input from the face. Both project to primary somatosensory cortex.
