ventral posterior thalamus.surg: Stroke here can give contralateral hemisensory loss and later central post-stroke pain (Dejerine-Roussy). Historically a target for pain stimulation; a landmark behind Vim in tremor surgery.

anterior thalamic nucleus.teach: Anterior group, beneath the anterior tubercle of the thalamus at the back of the foramen of Monro. It receives the mammillothalamic tract and projects to the cingulate gyrus (Papez circuit).
anterior thalamic nucleus.surg: Deep brain stimulation target for drug-resistant focal epilepsy. It forms the posterior margin of the foramen of Monro seen endoscopically.

mediodorsal thalamus.teach: Large medial nucleus reciprocally connected with prefrontal cortex and involved in executive function, working memory and affect.
mediodorsal thalamus.surg: Bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts (for example from an artery of Percheron occlusion) involving the mediodorsal nuclei produce memory and arousal disturbance.

centromedian / intralaminar thalamus.teach: Intralaminar nuclei, including the centromedian and parafascicular complex, lie within the internal medullary lamina and project widely to the striatum and cortex, supporting arousal and attention.
centromedian / intralaminar thalamus.surg: The centromedian nucleus is a deep brain stimulation target in generalised epilepsy (for example Lennox-Gastaut syndrome) and Tourette syndrome.

pulvinar.teach: Largest posterior thalamic nucleus, overhanging the midbrain and forming part of the wall of the atrium and quadrigeminal cistern. Connected with parietal, temporal and occipital association cortex for visual attention.
pulvinar.surg: Seen in posterior interhemispheric and supracerebellar approaches to the pineal region and atrium; posterior thalamic lesions often present on its surface.

geniculate body.teach: Lateral geniculate body: visual relay from the optic tract to the optic radiation. Medial geniculate body: auditory relay from the inferior colliculus to Heschl's gyrus. Both sit on the posterolateral thalamus beside the midbrain.
geniculate body.surg: The lateral geniculate is supplied by both anterior and posterior choroidal arteries, which explains characteristic sectoral field defects with vascular lesions. Both lie near the ambient cistern in subtemporal and transchoroidal approaches.

lateral dorsal / lateral posterior thala.teach: Dorsal tier nuclei of the lateral group, linked with cingulate and parietal association cortex; the lateral dorsal nucleus is often grouped functionally with the anterior (limbic) nuclei.
lateral dorsal / lateral posterior thala.surg: Mainly of anatomical interest; they lie beneath the floor of the body of the lateral ventricle.

ventral anterior thalamus.teach: Motor-related nucleus receiving pallidal and nigral output and projecting to premotor and prefrontal cortex.
ventral anterior thalamus.surg: Part of the pallidothalamic target region used in some thalamotomy and deep brain stimulation procedures for movement disorders.

limitans / suprageniculate thalamus.teach: Small posterior thalamic nuclei near the pretectum and geniculate bodies, with multisensory connections.

hypothalamus.teach: Forms the floor and lower lateral walls of the third ventricle below the hypothalamic sulcus. It is divided into anterior (preoptic/supraoptic), tuberal and posterior (mammillary) regions and controls endocrine, autonomic, temperature, appetite and sleep functions.
hypothalamus.surg: Injury during craniopharyngioma or suprasellar surgery can cause diabetes insipidus, hyperphagia and obesity, temperature and sleep disturbance. Preserving the hypothalamus is a major determinant of long-term outcome in these tumours.

pituitary.teach: Adenohypophysis (anterior lobe) and neurohypophysis (posterior lobe) in the sella turcica, connected by the infundibulum (stalk) to the hypothalamus. The anterior lobe secretes trophic hormones; the posterior lobe releases vasopressin and oxytocin made in the hypothalamus.
pituitary.surg: Pituitary adenomas are usually removed by the endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal route. Stalk or posterior lobe injury causes diabetes insipidus (sometimes as part of a triphasic response). The cavernous sinus and internal carotid arteries lie laterally and the optic chiasm above.

optic chiasm.teach: Partial crossing of the optic nerves above the pituitary: nasal retinal fibres (temporal visual fields) cross. Its position relative to the sella varies (prefixed, normal, postfixed).
optic chiasm.surg: Compression from below by pituitary or suprasellar tumours classically causes bitemporal hemianopia. Its relation to the tuberculum sellae and the corridors around it (prechiasmatic, opticocarotid) shape the choice of approach.

optic nerve.teach: Intraorbital, intracanalicular and intracranial segments run from the globe through the optic canal to the chiasm. It is a central nervous system tract covered by meninges.
optic nerve.surg: Unroofing the optic canal and opening the falciform ligament decompress it in tuberculum sellae and clinoidal meningiomas; the ophthalmic artery arises beneath it from the ICA.

optic tract.teach: Runs from the chiasm around the cerebral peduncle to the lateral geniculate body, carrying fibres serving the contralateral visual field.
optic tract.surg: Lesions give an incongruous contralateral homonymous hemianopia. It lies just below the globus pallidus internus (relevant to DBS) and along the medial edge of mesial temporal resections.

eyeball.teach: The globe, included here for orientation within the orbit alongside the extraocular muscles.
eyeball.surg: Reference point for orbital and transorbital approaches.

tectum.teach: The superior colliculi (visual orienting and vertical gaze) and inferior colliculi (auditory relay) form the roof of the midbrain behind the aqueduct; their brachia link them to the lateral and medial geniculate bodies.
tectum.surg: Tectal compression by pineal-region lesions produces Parinaud syndrome (upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus, light-near dissociation). Tectal plate gliomas are usually low grade and often managed by treating the hydrocephalus alone.

midbrain (part).teach: Part of the midbrain included as a separate label. The midbrain contains the cerebral peduncles, substantia nigra, tegmentum with red nuclei and oculomotor/trochlear nuclei, and the tectum around the aqueduct.
midbrain (part).surg: Surrounded by the interpeduncular, ambient and quadrigeminal cisterns, which are the corridors used to reach lesions on its surface.

lateral ventricle.teach: Paired C-shaped ventricles with frontal horn, body, atrium, occipital horn and temporal horn. The choroid plexus runs along the choroidal fissure from the foramen of Monro to the temporal horn and is largest at the atrium (glomus).
lateral ventricle.surg: Ventricular catheters are placed into the frontal horn via Kocher's point. Intraventricular tumours are approached transcallosally or transcortically depending on site; the atrium is reached through the superior parietal lobule or posterior interhemispheric routes.

temporal horn.teach: Inferior (temporal) horn of the lateral ventricle, in the medial temporal lobe; the hippocampus forms its floor and medial wall, and the amygdala lies at its tip.
temporal horn.surg: Entered in anterior temporal lobectomy and amygdalohippocampectomy. It dilates early in hydrocephalus and is a useful imaging sign; a trapped temporal horn can follow surgery near the trigone.

third ventricle.teach: Midline slit between the two thalami, with the hypothalamus in its floor and walls. It connects with the lateral ventricles through the foramina of Monro and with the fourth ventricle through the aqueduct.
third ventricle.surg: Reached by transcallosal-transforaminal, transchoroidal and interforniceal routes, or endoscopically. Its floor is fenestrated in endoscopic third ventriculostomy. Colloid cysts arise at its roof near the foramen of Monro.

fourth ventricle.teach: Diamond-shaped cavity behind the pons and upper medulla, beneath the cerebellum. Its floor (rhomboid fossa) carries the facial colliculus and the hypoglossal and vagal triangles; CSF exits through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie.
fourth ventricle.surg: Approached by the telovelar route, opening the tela choroidea and inferior medullary velum rather than splitting the vermis. Floor injury risks cranial nerve nuclei; brainstem mapping of the facial colliculus and hypoglossal triangle guides safe entry.

cerebral aqueduct.teach: Narrow channel through the midbrain linking the third and fourth ventricles, beneath the tectal plate.
cerebral aqueduct.surg: Aqueductal stenosis is a classic cause of obstructive hydrocephalus treated by endoscopic third ventriculostomy. Aqueductoplasty and stenting are used in selected cases.

cerebellar lobule.teach: Cerebellar lobule, numbered I to X from anterior to posterior (Larsell scheme); lobule VII is split into crus I, crus II and VIIB, and VIII into VIIIA and VIIIB. The labels here are subdivided into vermal and hemispheric zones. The anterior lobe (I-V) and lobule VIII carry sensorimotor maps, while crus I/II are connected with prefrontal and parietal association cortex.
cerebellar lobule.surg: Vermal and paravermal injury causes truncal ataxia; hemispheric lateral injury affects limb coordination. Extensive vermian splitting and bilateral dentate injury are linked to cerebellar mutism after posterior fossa tumour surgery in children, which is why the telovelar approach is preferred to the fourth ventricle.

dentate nucleus.teach: Largest deep cerebellar nucleus, in the white matter of each hemisphere near the roof of the fourth ventricle. It is the main output of the lateral cerebellum, projecting via the superior cerebellar peduncle to the red nucleus and ventral lateral thalamus.
dentate nucleus.surg: Bilateral dentate or dentatothalamocortical pathway injury is associated with cerebellar mutism syndrome; the nucleus lies at the lateral limit of telovelar and transvermian approaches.

fastigial / interposed nuclei.teach: Label grouping the deep cerebellar nuclei medial to the dentate: fastigial (vermal output to vestibular and reticular nuclei) and interposed (globose and emboliform, paravermal output to the red nucleus). The abbreviation appears to refer to fastigial, globose and emboliform nuclei; check the SPL atlas documentation for the exact definition.
fastigial / interposed nuclei.surg: Near the roof of the fourth ventricle, at risk in vermian approaches.

cerebellar white matter.teach: Cerebellar hemispheric white matter carrying afferent fibres (via the middle and inferior peduncles) and efferent fibres from the deep nuclei (via the superior peduncle).
cerebellar white matter.surg: Crossed in transcortical cerebellar approaches to hemispheric lesions and the fourth ventricle.

extraocular muscle.teach: Extraocular muscle. The four recti arise from the annulus of Zinn at the orbital apex; the superior oblique acts through the trochlea and the inferior oblique arises from the orbital floor. Innervation: lateral rectus by CN VI, superior oblique by CN IV, the rest (and levator palpebrae) by CN III.
extraocular muscle.surg: Orbital and transorbital approaches work between these muscles; the lateral rectus is the main landmark in lateral orbitotomy. Diplopia patterns help localise cranial nerve palsies from cavernous sinus, clival and brainstem lesions.

masticatory muscle.teach: Muscle of mastication (temporalis, masseter, medial and lateral pterygoid), all supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).
masticatory muscle.surg: Temporalis is reflected in frontotemporal and middle fossa craniotomies; the pterygoid muscles lie in the infratemporal fossa and are encountered in lateral skull-base and endoscopic transpterygoid approaches.

palatal and pharyngeal muscle.teach: Muscles of the soft palate and pharynx (tensor and levator veli palatini, palatoglossus, palatopharyngeus, stylopharyngeus, constrictors, uvula). Most are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus); tensor veli palatini by V3 and stylopharyngeus by CN IX.
palatal and pharyngeal muscle.surg: Landmarks in endoscopic endonasal and transoral approaches to the clivus and craniovertebral junction; the Eustachian tube and tensor/levator veli palatini mark the lateral limit of the nasopharyngeal corridor.

tongue.teach: Intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue (including hyoglossus), supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) apart from palatoglossus.
tongue.surg: Tongue deviation and atrophy indicate hypoglossal injury, relevant to foramen magnum, jugular foramen and high cervical surgery.

suboccipital muscle.teach: Deep suboccipital muscles (rectus capitis posterior major and minor, obliquus capitis superior and inferior) bound the suboccipital triangle, which contains the V3 segment of the vertebral artery and the C1 nerve.
suboccipital muscle.surg: These are key landmarks in far-lateral and posterior craniocervical exposures for locating the vertebral artery over the C1 arch.

posterior neck muscle.teach: Posterior cervical muscle (splenius, semispinalis, longissimus capitis, trapezius) forming the layered muscles of the back of the neck.
posterior neck muscle.surg: Divided in the midline or reflected in layers during posterior cervical and suboccipital approaches; anatomical closure reduces pseudomeningocele and CSF leak risk.

prevertebral muscle.teach: Longus colli, longus capitis and rectus capitis anterior lie on the front of the cervical spine and skull base behind the prevertebral fascia.
prevertebral muscle.surg: Longus colli is elevated laterally in anterior cervical discectomy to expose the uncovertebral joints; the sympathetic chain on its surface is at risk (Horner syndrome). Longus capitis is divided in endoscopic endonasal approaches to the lower clivus and craniovertebral junction.

neck muscle (other).teach: Neck muscle included for orientation (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, digastric, stylohyoid).
neck muscle (other).surg: Sternocleidomastoid and digastric are landmarks in far-lateral, retrosigmoid and jugular foramen approaches; the posterior belly of digastric runs close to the facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen.

facial muscle.teach: Muscle of facial expression, supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).
facial muscle.surg: Used to grade facial nerve function after cerebellopontine angle surgery (House-Brackmann grading).

hcp v1.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Primary visual cortex (V1), lining the calcarine sulcus. It receives the optic radiation and holds a retinotopic map of the contralateral visual field, with the macula at the occipital pole.
hcp v1.surg: Injury gives a contralateral homonymous field defect; see the optic radiation for the pathway leading here.

hcp 4.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Primary motor cortex (area 4) on the anterior bank of the central sulcus.
hcp 4.surg: Treated as eloquent; resections nearby are done with cortical and subcortical motor mapping.

hcp 3b.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Area 3b, the core primary somatosensory area in the posterior bank of the central sulcus (labelled "Primary Sensory Cortex" in HCPex).
hcp 3b.surg: Its position is confirmed intraoperatively by SSEP phase reversal across the central sulcus.

hcp 55b.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Area 55b: a small area between the frontal eye fields and ventral premotor cortex in the posterior middle frontal gyrus, newly described by the HCP-MMP study and implicated in language (it is part of the language network in task fMRI).
hcp 55b.surg: Its location varies between people, which is one reason individual mapping is needed for posterior middle frontal lesions in the dominant hemisphere.

hcp broca.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Area 44 (pars opercularis) or 45 (pars triangularis) of the inferior frontal gyrus; in the dominant hemisphere these form classical Broca's area.
hcp broca.surg: Awake language mapping is used for dominant-side lesions; stimulation-positive sites do not always coincide with the anatomical parcel.

hcp fef.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Frontal eye field (FEF) or premotor eye field (PEF): cortex controlling voluntary saccades and gaze, at the junction of the precentral sulcus with the superior (FEF) or inferior (PEF) frontal sulcus.
hcp fef.surg: Stimulation can produce contralateral eye deviation; transient gaze preference can follow resection.

hcp a1.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Primary auditory cortex (A1) on Heschl's gyrus.
hcp a1.surg: Unilateral injury rarely causes clinical deafness because hearing is represented bilaterally.

hcp hippocampus.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Hippocampal cortex (H) in the HCP-MMP scheme, part of the medial temporal section.
hcp hippocampus.surg: See the SPL hippocampus note for surgical relevance in mesial temporal epilepsy surgery.

hcp language.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Perisylvian language area (PSL) at the temporo-parietal junction, or superior frontal language area (SFL) on the medial superior frontal gyrus: both were identified in the HCP-MMP study as parts of the language network in task fMRI.
hcp language.surg: Illustrates that language cortex extends beyond the classical Broca and Wernicke regions; individual mapping is used rather than parcel boundaries.

hcp early visual.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Early visual. Early visual cortex (V2-V4) surrounding V1, with retinotopic maps and processing of form and colour.
hcp early visual.surg: Injury can produce quadrantic field defects or cerebral achromatopsia (ventral V4 region) depending on location.

hcp dorsal stream visual.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Dorsal stream visual. Dorsal-stream visual cortex (V3A, V3B, V6, V6A, V7, IPS1), processing spatial location and visual guidance of movement.
hcp dorsal stream visual.surg: Parieto-occipital injury can impair visually guided reaching (optic ataxia) and spatial perception.

hcp ventral stream visual.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Ventral stream visual. Ventral-stream visual cortex on the basal occipitotemporal surface (V8, VVC, PIT, FFC, VMV1-3), processing colour, objects, faces and written words.
hcp ventral stream visual.surg: Basal occipitotemporal resections can cause prosopagnosia, achromatopsia or alexia depending on side and site.

hcp mt+ complex and neighbouring visual.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: MT+ complex and neighbouring visual areas. MT+ complex and lateral occipital areas at the occipito-temporal junction (MT, MST, FST, V4t, LO1-3, V3CD, PH), specialised for visual motion and object shape.
hcp mt+ complex and neighbouring visual.surg: Bilateral injury near MT can cause akinetopsia (impaired motion perception). Lies above the optic radiation in lateral temporo-occipital approaches.

hcp somatosensory and motor.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Somatosensory and motor. Somatosensory-motor strip (areas 4, 3a, 3b, 1, 2) around the central sulcus.
hcp somatosensory and motor.surg: Peri-rolandic surgery uses motor and sensory mapping; see the precentral and postcentral gyrus notes.

hcp paracentral lobular and mid-cingulat.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Paracentral lobular and mid-cingulate. Paracentral lobule and mid-cingulate areas, including the supplementary motor area (6mp/6ma), supplementary and cingulate eye field, cingulate motor areas (24dd/24dv) and medial area 5.
hcp paracentral lobular and mid-cingulat.surg: SMA resection can cause a transient SMA syndrome (contralateral akinesia, reduced speech initiation on the dominant side).

hcp premotor.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Premotor. Premotor cortex (6d, 6a, 6v, 6r, together with 55b and the eye fields) in front of primary motor cortex, planning and selecting movements.
hcp premotor.surg: Ventral premotor cortex in the dominant hemisphere is often speech-positive on mapping (speech arrest or dysarthria).

hcp posterior opercular.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Posterior opercular. Posterior opercular cortex around the lower end of the central sulcus and parietal operculum (43, FOP1, OP1-4, PFcm), including secondary somatosensory cortex (SII) and vestibular regions.
hcp posterior opercular.surg: Opercular resections can cause face and tongue weakness or dysarthria; the parietal operculum is traversed in trans-opercular approaches to the posterior insula.

hcp early auditory.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Early auditory. Early auditory cortex: belt and parabelt areas around A1 on the supratemporal plane, plus retroinsular cortex.
hcp early auditory.surg: Crossed in trans-sylvian and superior temporal approaches; unilateral injury rarely affects hearing clinically.

hcp auditory association.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Auditory association. Auditory association cortex on the superior temporal gyrus and in the banks of the superior temporal sulcus (A4, A5, STS areas, STGa, TA2), supporting speech perception and, in the dominant hemisphere, language comprehension.
hcp auditory association.surg: Dominant posterior STG/STS resections risk receptive language deficits and are mapped awake.

hcp insular and frontal opercular.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Insular and frontal opercular. Insular and frontal opercular cortex: granular posterior insula (interoception, pain, temperature), agranular anterior insula (salience, autonomic and emotional integration), frontal operculum and piriform (olfactory) cortex.
hcp insular and frontal opercular.surg: See the insula note for surgical limits (M2 branches, lenticulostriate arteries, corticospinal tract).

hcp medial temporal.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Medial temporal. Medial temporal cortex: entorhinal, presubicular, perirhinal/ectorhinal and parahippocampal areas, the cortical gateway to the hippocampus for memory.
hcp medial temporal.surg: Resected in part during anterior temporal lobectomy and amygdalohippocampectomy; the extent of posterior parahippocampal resection influences memory outcome.

hcp lateral temporal.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Lateral temporal. Lateral and polar temporal cortex (TE1, TE2, PHT, TG), involved in semantic memory, naming and object knowledge.
hcp lateral temporal.surg: Dominant middle and inferior temporal resections are mapped for naming; the temporal pole is removed in standard anterior temporal lobectomy.

hcp temporo-parieto-occipital junction.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Temporo-parieto-occipital junction. Temporo-parieto-occipital junction (TPOJ1-3, STV, and PSL), a multimodal hub linked to language, social cognition and attention.
hcp temporo-parieto-occipital junction.surg: Dominant-side lesions here are mapped awake; non-dominant injury can contribute to neglect.

hcp superior parietal.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Superior parietal. Superior parietal and intraparietal areas (LIP, VIP, AIP, MIP, area 7 subdivisions), transforming visual and somatosensory information into eye, reach and grasp plans.
hcp superior parietal.surg: The superior parietal lobule is a standard corridor to the atrium; injury can cause optic ataxia or apraxia.

hcp inferior parietal.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Inferior parietal. Inferior parietal lobule areas (PF family on the supramarginal gyrus, PG family on the angular gyrus, IP0-2 in the intraparietal sulcus), supporting language, praxis, number processing and spatial attention.
hcp inferior parietal.surg: Dominant injury: conduction aphasia, alexia with agraphia or Gerstmann features. Non-dominant injury: neglect.

hcp posterior cingulate.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Posterior cingulate. Posterior cingulate, retrosplenial and precuneal cortex: core hubs of the default-mode network involved in memory, self-referential thought and navigation.
hcp posterior cingulate.surg: Traversed in posterior interhemispheric approaches; retrosplenial injury can cause topographical disorientation and memory impairment.

hcp anterior cingulate and medial prefro.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal. Anterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex (areas 24, 32, 33, 25, medial 8B, 9 and 10), involved in motivation, conflict monitoring, emotion regulation and autonomic control. Subgenual area 25 has been a deep brain stimulation target in depression research.
hcp anterior cingulate and medial prefro.surg: Bilateral injury can cause abulia or akinetic mutism; unilateral resection is usually tolerated. Relevant to interhemispheric approaches and anterior communicating aneurysm surgery.

hcp orbital and polar frontal.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Orbital and polar frontal. Orbitofrontal and frontopolar cortex (areas 10, 11, 13, orbital 47, OFC, pOFC), involved in reward valuation, decision making and social behaviour.
hcp orbital and polar frontal.surg: Subfrontal approaches retract this surface; the olfactory tract lies in the olfactory sulcus. Injury can cause disinhibition and personality change.

hcp inferior frontal.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Inferior frontal. Inferior frontal areas (44, 45, 47l, p47r, and inferior frontal junction and sulcus areas), including Broca's area on the dominant side.
hcp inferior frontal.surg: Mapped awake in the dominant hemisphere for naming, fluency and speech arrest.

hcp dorsolateral prefrontal.teach: HCP-MMP1 parcel (Glasser et al. 2016), shown here from the HCPex volumetric version. Section: Dorsolateral prefrontal. Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (areas 8, 9, 46, 9-46 and transitional 6-8 areas, together with SFL), supporting working memory, attention and executive control.
hcp dorsolateral prefrontal.surg: Unilateral resection rarely causes an obvious deficit, but executive and attentional changes may emerge on formal testing.

hcpex striatum/pallidum.teach: HCPex subcortical label. Basal ganglia nucleus (caudate, putamen, nucleus accumbens or globus pallidus); see the matching SPL structure for detail.
hcpex striatum/pallidum.surg: Globus pallidus internus is a deep brain stimulation target for dystonia and Parkinson's disease; the putamen is the commonest site of hypertensive haemorrhage.

jul hip.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Anterior intraparietal sulcus areas hIP1-3, involved in visuomotor transformation, number processing and attention.
jul hip.surg: Crossed in trans-sulcal routes along the intraparietal sulcus.

jul amyg.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Amygdala subdivision (laterobasal, centromedial or superficial group). The laterobasal group receives most sensory input; the centromedial group drives autonomic and behavioural output.
jul amyg.surg: Removed in mesial temporal resections; see the amygdala note.

jul broca.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Broca's region: area 44 (pars opercularis) or 45 (pars triangularis). Left-sided areas are typically larger and are part of the language network in most right-handed people.
jul broca.surg: Mapped awake in the dominant hemisphere; see the inferior frontal gyrus note.

jul hippo.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Hippocampal formation subdivision (cornu ammonis, dentate gyrus, subiculum, entorhinal cortex or the hippocampal-amygdaloid transition area).
jul hippo.surg: Hippocampal sclerosis mainly affects the CA1 and CA4 fields; see the hippocampus note for surgical relevance.

jul ipl.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Inferior parietal lobule area (PF, PFcm, PFm, PFop, PFt on the supramarginal gyrus; PGa, PGp on the angular gyrus).
jul ipl.surg: Dominant-side injury can affect language, praxis and calculation; non-dominant injury can cause neglect.

jul te.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Primary auditory cortex (TE1.0, TE1.1, TE1.2) on Heschl's gyrus.
jul te.surg: Unilateral injury rarely affects hearing clinically.

jul m1.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Primary motor cortex, area 4a (anterior) or 4p (posterior, in the depth of the central sulcus).
jul m1.surg: Eloquent; resections nearby use motor mapping.

jul s1.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Primary somatosensory cortex: area 3a (fundus of the central sulcus, proprioception), 3b (posterior bank, touch), 1 and 2 (crown of the postcentral gyrus).
jul s1.surg: Confirmed intraoperatively by SSEP phase reversal.

jul s2.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Parietal operculum areas OP1-OP4, containing secondary somatosensory cortex.
jul s2.surg: Traversed in trans-opercular approaches to the posterior insula.

jul spl.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Superior parietal lobule area (5Ci, 5L, 5M, 7A, 7M, 7P, 7PC).
jul spl.surg: The superior parietal lobule is a common route to the atrium.

jul vis.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Visual cortex area: V1 (area 17), V2 (area 18), V3v, V4 or V5/MT.
jul vis.surg: Injury produces field defects (V1/V2) or selective deficits such as achromatopsia (V4 region) or motion blindness (V5).

jul ba6.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Premotor cortex (area 6), including the supplementary motor area on the medial surface.
jul ba6.surg: SMA resection can cause a transient SMA syndrome.

jul insula.teach: Julich probabilistic cytoarchitectonic area (histology-based, Eickhoff/Amunts/Zilles group). Insular area: dysgranular Id1 or granular Ig1/Ig2 in the posterior insula.
jul insula.surg: See the insula note for surgical limits.

mni brain shell.teach: ICBM152 (2009c) template brain surface, shown translucent as spatial context for the co-registered overlay layers. It is an average of many brains, so individual gyri are smoothed.
